changes.after: Rust stores text as bytes. One written letter can take more than one byte.

before: String and str are UTF-8 text. len reports bytes, while chars iterates Unicode scalar values. A scalar value is not always a whole user-perceived character; grapheme segmentation needs additional rules.

str.get(range) returns Option<&str> and rejects out-of-range indices or non-character-boundary byte positions. Direct indexing with an invalid range can panic. In "éa", é occupies two bytes, so 0..2 selects it but 0..1 splits its encoding.

Expected output or behavior: 3 2
Some("é"). Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare bytes, chars and displayed characters without assuming they always have equal counts. You may trace it without a Rust compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: Rust stores text as bytes. One written letter can take more than one byte.
Here é takes two bytes. The range from byte 0 up to byte 2 contains the whole letter.
The output is `3 2`, then `Some("é")`. The two characters take three bytes. The requested slice ends between characters, so it succeeds.
Move the end of the range into the middle of é.

after.question: If the range changes to 0..1, what prints on the second line?
after.explanation: Byte 1 is inside é. A text slice cannot end there, so get returns None.
